title: Windows Event Logs
summary: Windows Event Logs are the structured, binary-encoded record stores in which the Windows operating system, its services and installed applications write timestamped events about authentication, process creation, service installation, policy change and errors. The mechanism matters because each event is written against a registered provider and channel, carries an event ID, and stores provider-specific data in a template that a consumer renders using the provider's manifest, so a log copied to another machine without that manifest can display as unreadable or misleading. In a real environment they are the primary evidence source for host-level incident response: the Security channel holds authentication and privilege events, System holds service and driver activity, PowerShell and Sysmon supply deeper process and command-line visibility, and they are collected centrally with forwarding or an agent because local logs are volatile and easily cleared. The mistake people usually make is grepping for event IDs without checking audit policy: if the relevant audit subcategory was never enabled, the absence of an event proves nothing at all, and default log sizes mean older records have already rolled away.

beginner.definition: Windows Event Logs are the diaries that Windows keeps about itself. The system, its services and your programs all write short numbered notes there. Each note has a time, a source and some details about what happened.
beginner.whyItMatters: When something goes wrong, the diary often shows what happened and in which order. A failed login, a new service or a stopped program all leave a note. Without these notes you are guessing, and the notes on the machine itself can be lost or deleted.
howItWorks: A program tells Windows that something worth recording has just happened.
Windows writes a numbered entry into the correct log channel.
The entry records the time, the source and the details about the event.
An administrator first turns on the categories of events to record.
Tools read the entries and can forward copies to a central server.
Analysts compare the entries from many machines to tell a story.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat with a notebook by the front door. Everyone writes down when they come home and who visited. If a bike goes missing, the flat reads the notebook backwards to see who entered that day. The notebook only helps if people actually wrote things down, and if nobody rips out pages.
takeaways: Event logs only contain what auditing was switched on to record.
Local logs are easy to clear, so forward copies to a central store.
An event ID is only meaningful together with its source and data.

objectives: Explain what Windows Event Logs record and which channels matter most.
Describe how audit policy determines which events exist at all.
Explain why event IDs alone can be misleading without the source and data.
Describe how central log collection improves evidence reliability.
Interpret common authentication and process-creation events during an investigation.
